*Ala rubba rakbin qad qata'tu wajifahum*
*ilayka wa lawla anta lam tawjifa al-rakbu*

(Many a riding party have I traversed, hastening them towards you; had it not been for you, the riding party would not have hastened.)

﴿But Allah gives power to His messengers over whom He wills.﴾ That is because fay' (spoils, property taken from the polytheists) is what is taken from the polytheists without fighting and without spurring on horses or camels. Allah therefore made it lawful for His Messenger to place it wherever he wills, because it comes through Allah giving the Messenger power over them, not through warring against them and subduing them.

Allah made this a provision for His Messenger, exclusively, apart from the people. He distributed it among the Muhajirun, except that Sahl ibn Hunayf and Abu Dujana mentioned poverty, so he gave to them both.

﴿So that it does not become a circulating wealth among the rich among you.﴾ It is said dawlah with a damma and with a fatha, and it has been recited with both. Regarding these two forms there are two opinions:

The first: they are one and the same. This was said by Yunus and al-Asma'i.

The second: there is a difference between them, and in this there are four aspects. (p-٥٠٤) The first: with fatha it means victory in war, and with damma it means wealth after poverty. This was said by Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala'.

The second: with fatha it refers to days, and with damma to wealth. This was said by Ubayda.

The third: with fatha it refers to what is like something settled, and with damma to what is like something borrowed. This was related by Ibn Kamil.

The fourth: with fatha it means a thrust in war, and with damma the days of kingship and the years which change. This was said by al-Farra'. Hassan said:

*Wa laqad niltum wa nilna minkum*
*wa kadhalika al-harbu ahyanan duwal*

(You have gained and we have gained from you, and so is war: at times it is a turn of fortune.)

﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it.﴾ In this there are four aspects:

The first: meaning, whatever he gives you of the property of fay', accept it, and whatever he withholds from you, do not seek it. This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: whatever Allah gives you of the property of ghanima (war booty), take it, and whatever He forbids you from, namely ghulu (misappropriation), do not do it. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: whatever He gives you of obedience to Me, do it, and whatever He forbids you of disobedience to Me, avoid it. This was said by Ibn Juraij.

The fourth: it is to be understood in its generality, covering all His commands and prohibitions, because He commands only what is good and forbids only what is corrupt.

﴿Seeking bounty from Allah and His good pleasure.﴾ That is, bounty from Allah's giving in this world, and good pleasure from His reward in the Hereafter.

It may carry a second meaning: that the "bounty" is sufficiency, and the "good pleasure" is contentment (qana'ah).

ʿAlī ibn Rabāḥ al-Lakhmī narrated that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb delivered a sermon at al-Jābiyah, saying: "Whoever wishes to ask about the obligatory shares of inheritance (al-farā'id), let him come to Zayd ibn Thābit. Whoever wishes to ask about jurisprudence (al-fiqh), let him come to Muʿādh ibn Jabal. Whoever wishes to ask about wealth (al-māl), let him come to me, for Allah the Exalted has made me a treasurer (khāzin) and a distributor (qāsim). I begin with the wives of the Prophet ﷺ, giving them their shares, then with the first Emigrants (al-Muhājirūn al-Awwalūn), myself and my companions, who were driven out of Makkah from our homes and our wealth."

Qatadah said: "Because they chose Allah and His Messenger ﷺ over the hardship they endured, to the extent that we were told a man would bind a stone upon his belly to straighten his spine from hunger, and a man would make a pit in winter, having no covering other than it."

The second view: the statement is to be taken in its apparent sense, its meaning being that they had settled in the abode and in faith before the Emigrants came to them, that is, by their welcoming them and sharing with them their wealth and dwellings.

The first: a jealousy (ghayrah and ḥasad) over the precedence and nearness they were given, and this is a possible reading.

The second: that is, envy over what the Emigrants were singled out for from the spoils of fay' and other things, so they do not envy them for it. This was said by al-Ḥasan.

﴿And they prefer them over themselves, even though they themselves were in dire need﴾. That is, they prefer them and give them precedence over themselves, even though they had poverty and need. From this is the saying of the poet:

"As for spring, when there is need (khaṣāṣah), the sick man lives by it, and the poor man becomes rich."

Concerning their preference (ithār) there are two views:

The first: they preferred the Emigrants over themselves with what came of fay' and booty, to the point that it was divided among the Emigrants without them. This was said by Mujāhid and Ibn Ḥayyān.

It is narrated that the Prophet ﷺ distributed among the Emigrants what Allah had granted as fay' from the Banū al-Naḍīr, and gave a share (nafl) from Qurayẓah on the condition that the Emigrants would return to the Anṣār what they had given them of their wealth. The Anṣār said: "Rather, we shall maintain for them from our wealth, and prefer them with the fay'." So Allah revealed this verse.

The second: they preferred the Emigrants with their wealth and shared it with them.

Ibn Zayd narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said to them: "Your brothers have left their wealth and children and came out to you." They said: "Our wealth is between them as shares." He said: "Or is it not so?" They said: "And what is that, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "They are a people who do not know work, so you shall provide for them and share the dates with them," meaning from what came to them from the palm groves of Banū al-Naḍīr. They said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah."
